analysis.one_liner: Requires mandatory government safety testing so dressers and chests cannot tip over on children.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill requiring the CPSC to write binding anti-tip-over tests for dressers — with 16 Senate cosponsors including 2 Republicans — never left the Senate Commerce Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The STURDY Act would have ordered the Consumer Product Safety Commission to replace voluntary furniture guidelines with a binding federal safety rule for dressers, bureaus, and chests of drawers. The rule would have to test whether units stay upright when a child up to 60 pounds climbs or pulls on them, including on carpet with drawers open and loaded, and it would have covered shorter units that were previously exempt from testing. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in February 2021 and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children, who are the main victims of dresser tip-overs — children climbing or pulling on unanchored dressers can be crushed. A binding standard with realistic climbing tests would force manufacturers to sell only units that stay standing under those conditions, and would require clear tip-over warnings on every unit sold in the U.S. Parents would no longer have to rely on voluntary industry standards that the bill directed the CPSC to assess and, where necessary, strengthen.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the CPSC to issue a final, legally binding safety standard for freestanding clothing storage units within one year, with tests simulating a child weighing up to 60 pounds, and accounting for carpet, loaded drawers, multiple open drawers, and dynamic force — conditions closer to how children actually use furniture.
Extends mandatory testing to all clothing storage units, including those under 30 inches tall, closing a gap in the voluntary standard.
Requires tip-over warning labels based on the ASTM F2057-17 standard, with the CPSC required to strengthen them if reasonably necessary to protect children.

Makes the standard self-updating: if the CDC revises its growth charts, the weight simulation must rise to the 95th percentile weight for a 6-year-old unless the CPSC specifically finds that unnecessary.

analysis.who_pays: Furniture manufacturers and importers, who would bear the cost of the new testing, any redesign needed to pass it, and warning labels for every clothing storage unit sold in the U.S. Small craft and handmade furniture makers — whom the bill specifically required the CPSC to consult — would face the same testing burden relative to their size. Some of these costs would likely be passed on to shoppers as higher dresser prices.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory testing and any resulting redesign would raise compliance costs for manufacturers, and particularly for small craft and handmade furniture makers, with some share likely showing up as higher prices for consumers.

A binding federal rule would replace the existing voluntary standard (ASTM F2057-17) that industry already followed, so the bill imposes a new regulatory floor on a market that had been governed by industry-set guidelines — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge, justified by the argument that the voluntary standard did not test real-world climbing conditions like carpet and loaded drawers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — keeping unstable dressers from crushing children — is significant and the cost, while real for manufacturers and small furniture makers, is the ordinary price of mandatory product testing that many consumer products already undergo. The bill was designed to limit overreach by requiring consultation with manufacturers, craft makers, and independent engineers, and by letting the CPSC modify the rule later if it found that unnecessary. On its face the benefits outweigh the costs; the bill's failure means the question was never tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee never took the bill up after referring it, and it quietly died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Bob Casey introduced the STURDY Act on February 25, 2021, joined by 14 other original senators from both parties, including Republican Tom Cotton.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the record for the rest of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Furniture manufacturers and importers are better off, because they never had to meet mandatory tip-over testing, redesign, or labeling requirements. Families with young children are worse off, since no binding federal standard resulted from this bill.

for.name: Sen. Bob Casey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: 2 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record for the entire two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 14 of 48 Democrats and 2 of 50 Republicans signed on — but the bill never reached a floor vote, so partisan support was never actually tested.

industries.note: The bill would have required testing, and possibly redesign, of every freestanding clothing storage unit sold in the U.S. — including the large share that is imported. The industry's interest in avoiding mandatory compliance costs runs against children's safety, though the bill did require the CPSC to consult with manufacturers in writing the rule.

industries.industry: Small craft and handmade furniture makers
industries.note: The bill singled out craft and handmade furniture makers for consultation but did not exempt them from the testing and warning requirements, so the same compliance burden would fall on them relative to their smaller scale.

Retailers could only sell units meeting the new standard, which would have meant clearing noncompliant stock and relying on certified suppliers — a cost, but one passed through from the same safety rule that protects their customers' children.
